subject: Agriculture
title: How Soil Holds Water
description: A quick win: understand How Soil Holds Water.

hook.text: Pour water on sand and it drains instantly. Pour it on clay and it sits there for days. Why?

buildup.text: Water clings to soil particles by surface tension. Smaller particles have more surface area, so they hold more.

discovery.text: Field capacity is the sweet spot—soil holds enough water for roots but has drained excess. Plants thrive here.

twist.text: Wilting point is when water clings too tightly to particles for roots to extract it. The plant dies of thirst.

climax.text: Good farm management keeps soil moisture between field capacity and wilting point—the plant-available zone.

punchline.text: Soil holds water. The art is holding just enough.

quiz.question: What is the 'wilting point' in soil science?
options: When the soil dries out completely
When water clings too tightly to particles for roots to absorb it
When plants have too much water

details.summary: Soil holds water in pore spaces through a balance of gravitational drainage, capillary forces, and adhesion to particle surfaces. This topic covers field capacity, permanent wilting point, and available water capacity—the concepts that determine how much water crops can actually access.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding soil water dynamics is essential for irrigation scheduling and crop management. The difference between field capacity and wilting point—the available water capacity—determines how long crops can survive between rain or irrigation.
takeaways: Field capacity is the amount of water soil holds after free drainage has stopped
Permanent wilting point is when remaining water is held too tightly for roots to extract
Available water capacity varies from 25mm per meter depth in sand to 200mm in loam

faq.question: What determines how much water soil can hold for crops?
faq.answer: Soil texture and organic matter are the main factors. Clay soils hold the most total water but much is held too tightly for roots. Sandy soils hold little water but most is available. Loamy soils with good organic matter provide the best balance of total and available water.

faq.question: What is the difference between field capacity and wilting point?
faq.answer: Field capacity is the water remaining after gravity drains excess—it is the soil's full 'tank.' Permanent wilting point is when the remaining water is bonded so tightly to soil particles that roots cannot extract it. The difference between these two values is the available water crops can use.
